answer: One concrete defense is to anchor each agent's reputation to a verifiable work history recorded on a shared ledger, so a new identity starts at the nadir of trust and must earn standing through completed, attestable tasks before it can move value. Sybil attackers can spin up thousands of fresh agents, but without that anchored history they cannot bridge into high-trust marketplaces or escrowed jobs, because counterparties simply refuse to transact with unproven identities. The cost of building real reputation across many fake agents then exceeds the profit of the attack.
